items.html: Euge! Euge, euge! — Bravo! (Plaut. Mil. 241b; Ter. Ad. 911). Fēcī! — I did it!

collīneō (conl-), collīneāre — aim straight, hit the mark (rare; Cicero): quis est enim, quī tōtum diem jaculāns nōn aliquandō conlīniet? — “who throws all day without sometimes hitting the mark?” (Cic. Div. 2.121, the edition’s form). Collīneāvī! — Bullseye!

Tetigistī acū! — Spot on! literally “you touched it with a needle” (Plaut. Rud. 1306b, where Labrax admits he is one letter more than a medicus: a mendīcus). The later school dialogues expand it to Rem acū tetigistī (Cordier, Schottenius).
Paene! — Almost! Paene fēcistī! — You almost did it!

Minimum āfuit quīn facerēs! — You came within a hair of doing it! (cf. minimum āfuit quīn perīret, Suet. Aug. 14; paulum āfuit quīn, Caes. B.C. 2.35). The short Minimum āfuit! — So close! — is our ellipsis.
Frūstrā! — Missed! Nōn tetigī. — I didn’t hit it. Both ours: aberrāre means to stray from the way and is not attested of a missed throw, and in the school dialogues Errāvī means “I made a mistake.”

items.html: tympanum, tympanī n. — drum; tympanum pulsāre — play the drum (Traupman 53, 168; M-O s.v. percussion: drum; Catull. 63).
tuba, tubae f. — trumpet; tubā canere (Traupman 41, 168; M-O s.v. brass: trumpet).
tībia, tībiae f. — pipe, flute (Traupman 168, 317); classically the reed pipe. Morgan–Owens distinguishes tībia oblīqua (flute) and tībia rēcta (recorder, M-O s.v. winds).

cithara (Hispānica) — guitar (Traupman 168; M-O s.v. guitar); citharā canere. The ancient cithara is a lyre.

violin: Traupman’s fidicula (168) is in Lewis & Short only as the plural fidiculae, fidiculārum f. — a small lyre (Cic.), and also an instrument of torture. Morgan–Owens gives violīnum (M-O s.v. strings1: violin, modern).

tintinnābulum, tintinnābulī n. — bell (Plaut.; Juv.); tintinnābulum pulsāre — ring a bell (M-O s.v. bell).

sībilus, sībilī m. — whistle, the sound; sībilum ēmittere — blow the whistle (Traupman 45). Neither source has a settled word for the toy whistle (M-O s.v. whistle (device) offers a doubtful fistella).

english: Puppets, clowns and tricks: puppet / clown / magician / magic tricks / juggler / acrobat / tightrope walker / circus / amusement park
latin: neurospaston, neurospastī n. · joculātor, joculātōris m.
keywords: puppet marionette puppet show clown jester magician conjuror magic tricks juggler acrobat tumbler tightrope walker circus amusement park funfair

items.html: neurospaston, neurospastī n. — puppet, marionette, “a figure set in motion by strings” (Gell. 14.1.23; L&S). Morgan–Owens agrees (neurospastum, M-O s.v. puppet: marionette); Traupman 367 misprints it neuropastum.
joculātor, joculātōris m. — clown, jester (M-O s.v. clown; L&S: rare but classical, Cic. Att. 4.16.3). Morgan–Owens also lists scurra and, for a court fool, mōriō.

praestigiātor, praestigiātōris m. — conjuror, magician; praestigiae, praestigiārum f. pl. — conjuring tricks (M-O s.v. magician; magic; Plaut.; L&S: ante-classical and post-Augustan). Traupman gives magus, magī m. (343), properly a Persian priest or sorcerer, and praestigiārī — do tricks (167).

pilārius, pilāriī m. — juggler (M-O s.v. ball-player: juggler; Quint. 10.7.11); petaurista, petauristae m. — acrobat, tumbler (M-O s.v. acrobat); fūnambulus, fūnambulī m. — tightrope walker (Traupman 163; M-O; Ter. Hec. prol. 4).
lūdī pāpiliōnāriī — circus (M-O s.v. circus, a modern coinage from medieval pāpiliō, a tent). Classical circus is the race-course, a false friend.
hortī pūblicī oblectāriī — amusement park (Traupman 51, 271). oblectārius is not in Lewis & Short; the Vatican lexicon’s hortī pūblicī oblectātōriī uses oblectātōrius (Gell.) instead.
Praestigiātor nummum ex aure tuā prōmpsit! — The magician took a coin out of your ear!
Spectā fūnambulum: nōn cadit! — Look at the tightrope walker: he doesn’t fall!

blocks.html: Lewis & Short marks the i of praestigiae as doubtful; Traupman and Morgan–Owens print it long. It is left unmarked here.

english: Cards and board games: riddle / playing cards / shuffle / deal / board / counter / dice / chess / draughts
latin: chartula lūsōria · tabula lūsōria · aenigma, aenigmatis n.
keywords: riddle puzzle quiz cards playing cards card game shuffle deal board game game board counter piece dice die knucklebones chess draughts checkers

items.html: aenigma, aenigmatis n. — riddle, puzzle (Traupman 367; Cic.; Quint.); the Vatican lexicon uses it for a quiz. Neither source has a word for a jigsaw.

playing card: Traupman gives chartula lūsōria and chartulīs lūdere (51); Morgan–Owens gives charta lūsōria, folium lūsōrium, chartīs lūdere (M-O s.v. card: playing card, from Vives 1540). chartās miscēre — shuffle; chartās distribuere — deal (both sources).
tabula lūsōria — game board (M-O s.v. playing board; Mart. 14.17); calculus, calculī m. — counter, playing piece (M-O s.v. playing piece), the classical word for a gaming stone.
tesserae, tesserārum f. pl. — dice; tālī, tālōrum m. pl. — knucklebones (L&S). tesserīs lūdere — play dice. Neither book has these in the sections swept. In the lexicon tessera is also a ticket.
chess: Traupman gives lūdus scācōrum and scācīs lūdere (51–52); Morgan–Owens gives medieval scaccī, scaccōrum m. pl. (M-O s.v. chess, from Ducange).

draughts, checkers: Traupman uses latrunculī and latrunculīs lūdere (51); Morgan–Owens uses latrunculī for chess and gives lūdus damicus for draughts (M-O s.v. checkers). The Roman game of latrunculī (Sen. Ep. 106.11 latrunculīs lūdimus) was a third, distinct game.
Chartās miscē; ego distribuam. — You shuffle the cards; I’ll deal.
Tesserās jace! — Throw the dice!
Aenigma tibi prōpōnam: quid est? — I’ll give you a riddle: what is it?

english: Sport and exercise: gym / exercise / jog / skipping / race / team / referee / win / lose / point / score / draw
latin: exercitātiō, exercitātiōnis f. · vincō, vincere, vīcī, victum

items.html: gymnasium, gymnasiī n. — gym (Traupman 48); palaestra, palaestrae f. — gym, exercise ground (M-O s.v. gym; Plaut.; Cic.).
exercitātiō, exercitātiōnis f. — exercise; sē exercēre — exercise, work out (Traupman 45, 83; M-O s.v. exercise; Cic.).
cursitāre — jog (M-O s.v. jog; L&S: run about, rare); Traupman 84 gives tolūtim cursitāre, to jog at a trot. ad fūnem salīre — skip, jump rope (Traupman 83).
curriculum, curriculī n. — race, also the race-track (Traupman 50; M-O s.v. race); certāmen cursūs — running race (Traupman 368).
turma, turmae f. — team (Traupman 45, 391; classically a cavalry squadron); Morgan–Owens gives manus, manūs f., a band (M-O s.v. team). arbiter, arbitrī m. — referee (Traupman 44–45).
lūdō vincere — win a game (Traupman 44, 407; M-O s.v. win a game, from Vives: lūdum vincere); lūdō superārī; lūdum perdere — lose a game (Traupman 44).

pūnctum, pūnctī n. — point; pūnctum ferre — score a point; summa pūnctōrum — the score; Summae pūnctōrum sunt parēs. — The score is level (Traupman 44–45, 375). Morgan–Owens gives numerus for a point and aequālitās numerōrum for a draw (M-O s.v. score).
Quis vīcit? — Nēmō: summae pūnctōrum sunt parēs. — Who won? — Nobody: it’s a draw.
Ad fūnem salī: ūnum, duo, tria … — Skip: one, two, three …
Ad arborem certēmus cursū! — Let’s race to the tree!

items.html: traha, trahae f.; trahea, traheae f. — sledge, sled (M-O s.v. sled, sleigh, traha, from Columella; Traupman 75, 134, 380 trahea, Verg. G. 1.164); traheā vehī — go sledging (Traupman 75, 380); Interdum dē colle traheā lābimur. — Sometimes we slide down the hill on a sledge (Traupman 134).
pila nivis — snowball (Traupman 136); pilās nivis inter nōs conjicimus — we throw snowballs at each other (Traupman 134).
vir nivis — snowman; virum nivis facere — build a snowman (Traupman 134).
narta, nartae f. — ski; nartāre — ski; nartātor, nartātōris m. — skier (Traupman 49, 380; M-O s.v. ski, skier, modern; the Vatican lexicon agrees on nartātor).

ice skates: Traupman gives patinī and patināre (48–49, 331), coined on Italian pattinare (classical patina is a dish). Morgan–Owens gives solea ferrea and soleā ferreā lūdere (M-O s.v. skate: ice-skate, from Egger); the Vatican lexicon gives ferrāta solea.
calceī subrotātī — roller skates; tabula subrotāta — skateboard (Traupman 49, 380; M-O s.v. skate: roller-skate; skateboard; subrotātus is Vitruvian).
Virum nivis faciāmus! — Let’s build a snowman!
Trahā dē colle lābāmur! — Let’s sledge down the hill!
Nōlī pilam nivis in faciem cujusquam conjicere. — Don’t throw a snowball in anyone’s face.

keywords: camera photo photograph picture take a photo television TV watch TV cartoon cartoons film movie cinema radio remote control video game computer game comics comic book

items.html: māchinula phōtographica — camera (Traupman 51, 286; M-O s.v. camera); Traupman also gives phōtomāchina. imāgō phōtographica — photo (both). take a photo: Traupman gives phōtographicē reddere (53), Morgan–Owens imāginem lūce imprimere (M-O s.v. photograph (vi)).

tēlevīsiō, tēlevīsiōnis f. — television; tēlevīsiōnem spectāre — watch TV (Traupman 53). For the set, Traupman gives tēlevīsōrium and Morgan–Owens īnstrūmentum tēlevīsificum (M-O s.v. television). moderātrum remōtum — remote control (Traupman 53).
spectāculum animātum — cartoon (Traupman 51).

pellicula cinēmatographica — film (Traupman 52; M-O s.v. movie, film). cinema: Traupman gives cinēmatēum (52), Morgan–Owens theātrum cinēmatographicum; M-O argues that cinēmatographēum ought to mean a film studio (M-O s.v. movie theater).
radiophōnum, radiophōnī n. — radio (Traupman 53; M-O s.v. radio); the Vatican lexicon gives radiophōnium.
lūsus computātrālis — computer game (Traupman 295), which fits the lexicon’s computātrum; lūsus magnētoscopicus (Traupman 402) is the older VCR-era term.
libellī pīctographicī — comics (Traupman 294).
Stā immōtus: tē phōtographicē reddam. — Stand still: I’ll take your photo.
Ūnum tantum spectāculum animātum, deinde dormītum. — Just one cartoon, then bed.
